zh: 第三、明體用，即為二意：一者、明因果；二、明體用。一、因果者，遠而論之，行內外方便及入未到地等為因，感得初禪為果。今就近釋，但據初禪，自有因果。有人言：「四支為因，後一心支為果。」此即無文。今依《纓絡》解禪支，五支為因，第六默然心為定體，即以體為果。若通論因果，支支相因，悉得辨因果也。
en: Third, clarifying substance and function: this itself has two parts — clarifying cause and effect; and clarifying substance and function.

First, as for cause and effect: discussed broadly, cultivating the external and internal expedient means and entering the "not-yet-arrived" state and the rest serve as the cause, and attaining the first dhyāna as its result serves as the effect. Discussed narrowly, however, the first dhyāna alone has its own cause and effect. Some say: "the four factors serve as the cause, and the subsequent factor of one-pointedness of mind serves as the effect" — but this has no textual basis. Here, following the Yingluo Sūtra's own explanation of the dhyāna-factors, the five factors serve as the cause, and the sixth, the mind of silence, serves as the substance of concentration — taking this substance itself as the effect. Discussed generally, cause and effect may be found in every factor causing the next in turn.

zh: 二、明體用，還以默然心為定體，從默然觸更動發起五支，此則為用。何以故？從體起用，用則在後，因則據前。問曰：因用體果，即無分別。答曰：不然。雖同據五支明因用，就默然為體果，然義意有異。所以者何？因中五支，為感默然之果。因默然之果，起五支之法。此就默然為體，五支為用。例如三十七品，道前為因，道後為用。問曰：有時從默然體發勝品五支，後得增勝默然，此義云何？答曰：若爾，即還應說因果，若無勝品，但是體用。
en: Second, clarifying substance and function: taking the mind of silence once again as the substance of concentration, from this silent contact the five factors are further stirred and brought forth — this, then, is the function. Why is this? Function arises from substance, and so function comes afterward while cause is what precedes it. Question: if cause and function, substance and effect, are thus paired, is there then no distinction between them at all? Answer: this does not follow. Although the five factors are used, in both cases, to clarify cause and function, and silence to clarify substance and effect, their sense nonetheless differs. Why is this? Within the sense of cause, the five factors serve to bring about the effect of silence. Within the sense of function, it is the effect of silence that gives rise to the dharma of the five factors — here, silence serves as substance, and the five factors serve as function. This is comparable to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment: what precedes the path serves as cause, and what follows the path serves as function. Question: at times, from the substance of silence, a superior grade of the five factors is brought forth, and afterward an even more excellent silence is attained — what is the sense of this? Answer: if this is so, then cause and effect should indeed be spoken of once again; but where there is no superior grade involved, it is simply a matter of substance and function.

This section's real subtlety is that the same five factors get assigned opposite roles depending on the frame: as cause, they bring about the substance of silence as their effect; as function, that very same substance of silence is what gives rise to them. Nothing here is inconsistent — it is the same relationship viewed forward (cause producing effect) and backward (substance expressing itself as function) — but the treatise is careful to flag exactly when a second, genuine cause-and-effect relationship reappears within what would otherwise be a single substance-and-function cycle: whenever a superior grade of the five factors leads to a genuinely more excellent silence than before, rather than simply re-expressing the same one.

items.en: Depth, Progress and Regression, and Merits
items.zh: 初禪 · 明淺深、進退、功德
parent: The First Dhyāna: Marks of Realization

zh: 第四、明淺深者，初禪發時，五支及默然心前後不無麁細之異，故有淺深，應須分別。所以者何？如論云：「佛弟子修諸禪時，有下、中、上，名為三品。離此三品，一品為三，故有九品淺深之相。若細而論，則應有無量品。」外道得定亦有淺深，而不作品說者，以其心麁，於定中不覺故，亦以不修無漏觀慧照了，則心不覺知。就立品明淺深中，自為二意：一、約同類；二、約異類。一、同類者，如一動觸發時，漸漸覺深，乃至九品；二、約異類者，如動觸謝後，即發餘觸，雖觸相不同，而覺定漸深勝於上。復次，若約五支中明淺深者，亦有二：一、同類者，如觸發五支時，即有淺深之相；二、異類者，若五支次第增長，一一支中亦各自有淺深之相。
en: Fourth, clarifying depth: when the first dhyāna arises, the five factors and the mind of silence are not without their own differences of coarseness and fineness from one moment to the next, and so there is shallowness and depth, which must be properly distinguished. Why is this? As the treatise says: "When the Buddha's disciples cultivate the various dhyānas, there is a lower, a middle, and an upper grade, named the three grades; and, separating out each of these three grades into three further grades in turn, there are nine grades of shallowness and depth in all. Examined finely, there should be measureless grades beyond even this." Non-Buddhist practitioners, too, attain concentrations with their own shallowness and depth, though this is not spoken of in terms of grades for them, since their minds are coarse, unable to perceive it within concentration itself, and, not cultivating the uncontaminated wisdom that illuminates it, the mind fails to become aware of it at all.

Within establishing these grades to clarify depth, there are, in turn, two senses: with reference to the same kind; and with reference to differing kinds. As for the same kind: as when the single sensation of movement arises, one becomes aware of it growing gradually deeper, all the way through nine grades. As for differing kinds: as when, once the sensation of movement has passed, some other sensation then arises in turn — although the marks of the sensations differ, the sense of concentration nonetheless grows gradually deeper, surpassing what came before. Furthermore, with reference to the five factors, depth may likewise be clarified in two senses: with reference to the same kind, as when the five factors arise together with a given sensation, there is already a mark of shallowness and depth present; and with reference to differing kinds, as when the five factors grow and increase one after another in sequence, each single factor, in turn, also has its own mark of shallowness and depth.

zh: 問曰：為當要發十六觸等具足，方名初禪，為當亦發一一觸亦名初禪？答曰：初禪有二種：一、具足；二、不具足。若具發十六觸，此即是具足初禪為勝；若發一兩觸等，亦得名初禪。何以故？以一觸具有十種定法，眷屬五支成就故，但此初禪不名具足。
en: Question: must all sixteen tactile sensations arise together, complete in full, before something can be named the first dhyāna — or can even a single sensation arising also be named the first dhyāna? Answer: the first dhyāna is of two kinds: complete; and incomplete. If all sixteen sensations arise together in full, this is precisely the complete first dhyāna, and is superior; but if only one or two sensations arise, this too may be named the first dhyāna. Why is this? Because even a single sensation is already complete with the ten dharmas of concentration, its retinue of five factors already accomplished — it is simply that this form of the first dhyāna is not called "complete."

zh: 第五、明進退者，證初禪時，有四種人根性不同：一者、退分；二者、住分；三者、進分；四者、達分。一、退分者，若人得初禪時，或有因緣，或無因緣，而便退失。失有二種：一者、更修還得；二者、更修不得。所謂過去今世障法起故，末世之中，此退分多。二、住分者，有人得初禪已，即不退失，定心安隱。住分亦有二種：一者、任運自住；二者、守護乃住。三、進分者，有人得初禪時，即便進得勝品，乃至進得上地。進有二種：一者、不加功力，任運自進；二者、勤修乃進。四、達分者，有人得初禪時，於此定中即發見思無漏，達到涅槃。達亦有二種：一者、任運自達；二者、修觀乃達。
en: Fifth, clarifying progress and regression: at the time the first dhyāna is realized, there are four kinds of practitioner, differing in capacity — those prone to regression; those who abide; those who progress; and those who penetrate through.

First, as for those prone to regression: some people, upon attaining the first dhyāna, whether through some cause and condition or through none at all, regress and lose it. This loss is of two kinds: regaining it through further cultivation; or failing to regain it even through further cultivation, owing to some obstructing dharma from the past or the present life. In this latter age, those prone to regression of this kind are many.

Second, as for those who abide: some people, having attained the first dhyāna, do not regress or lose it at all, the concentrated mind remaining secure. Abiding, too, is of two kinds: abiding spontaneously, of its own accord; and abiding only through guarding and protecting it.

Third, as for those who progress: some people, upon attaining the first dhyāna, immediately progress further to a superior grade, and even progress all the way to a higher stage. Progress, too, is of two kinds: progressing spontaneously, without any application of effort; and progressing only through diligent cultivation.

Fourth, as for those who penetrate through: some people, upon attaining the first dhyāna, within this very concentration, at once bring forth the uncontaminated attainment of the path of vision and the path of cultivation, penetrating through all the way to nirvāṇa. This too is of two kinds: penetrating through spontaneously, of its own accord; and penetrating through only through cultivating contemplation.

zh: 復次，此四分定中，復有四種人根性不同，如退分中四者：一、自有退退得，九品漸退，乃至併失；二、自有退住得，九品退至八品、七品，便住不失；三、自有退進得，九品退至八品、七品，乃至一品，從一品還進；四者、自有退達得，九品已退，還八、七等品，乃至一品，於其中間忽然發真無漏。餘住分、進分、達分各有四義亦如是。是中或有因放逸障故退，或因懺悔清淨故住、進、達，此義眾多，不可具辨。
en: Furthermore, within these four divisions of concentration, there are, in turn, four further kinds of practitioner differing in capacity, exactly as the four given within the "prone to regression" division: some regress and, having regressed, remain merely at regression — the nine grades gradually regressing, all the way to total loss; some regress and, having regressed, come to abide — the nine grades regressing to the eighth or seventh grade, and then abiding there without further loss; some regress and, having regressed, come to progress — the nine grades regressing to the eighth or seventh grade, or even to the first grade, and then progressing forward again from that first grade; and some regress and, having regressed, come to penetrate through — the nine grades having already regressed back to the eighth, seventh, or even the first grade, and then, in the midst of this very interval, suddenly bringing forth the true uncontaminated attainment. The remaining divisions — abiding, progressing, and penetrating through — each likewise have these same four further senses. Among these, regression may occur due to the obstruction of heedlessness, or abiding, progress, and penetration may occur due to the purity brought about through repentance — this sense is itself manifold, and cannot be distinguished here in full.

zh: 第六、明初禪功德者，如前偈說：「已得離婬火，則獲清涼定。」此偈自可為二功德：一者、離過德；二者、善心德。此對止、行二善，亦可類於智、斷二德，故《大集經》云：「初禪者，亦名為離，亦名為具。所言離者，謂離五蓋；所言具者，謂具五支。」今釋所以得初禪時離貪欲蓋者，欲界之樂麁淺，今得初禪之樂細妙，以勝奪輕，故能離五欲。離瞋者，欲界苦緣逼迫故生瞋，得初禪時，無有諸逼迫，樂境在心，故無瞋。能離睡眠者，得初禪時，身心明淨，定法所持，心不昏亂，觸樂自娛，故不睡也。所以能離掉悔者，禪定持心，任運不動，故能離掉。由掉故有悔，無掉即無悔。離疑者，未得初禪時，疑有定、無定，今親證定，疑心即除，故得離疑，是故得初禪時具有離過之德。
en: Sixth, clarifying the merit of the first dhyāna: as the verse already cited above says, "Having already gained freedom from the fire of lust, one obtains a cool, refreshing concentration." This verse may itself be understood as two kinds of merit: the merit of freedom from fault; and the merit of a wholesome mind. This corresponds to the two forms of wholesomeness, stopping and practice, and may likewise be compared to the two merits of wisdom and severance. Hence the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says: "The first dhyāna is named both 'freedom' and 'completeness.' As for 'freedom': this means freedom from the five hindrances. As for 'completeness': this means completeness in the five factors."

Here, it is explained why, upon attaining the first dhyāna, one gains freedom from the hindrance of craving: the pleasure of the desire realm is coarse and shallow, while the pleasure now attained through the first dhyāna is fine and subtle — the superior displacing the inferior, and so one is able to gain freedom from the five desires. As for gaining freedom from anger: within the desire realm, the oppressive conditions of suffering give rise to anger; upon attaining the first dhyāna, there is no such oppression present at all, and, with a state of happiness held in the mind, there is no anger. As for being able to gain freedom from drowsiness: upon attaining the first dhyāna, body and mind grow bright and pure, sustained by the dharma of concentration, the mind no longer dull or disordered, delighting of itself in the joy of the tactile sensation — hence there is no drowsiness. As for being able to gain freedom from restlessness and regret: dhyāna-concentration sustains the mind, unmoved of its own accord, and so one is able to gain freedom from restlessness; and since regret arises on account of restlessness, where there is no restlessness, there is no regret either. As for gaining freedom from doubt: before attaining the first dhyāna, one doubts whether concentration exists or not; now, having personally realized concentration, the doubting mind is thereby removed — hence one gains freedom from doubt as well. Hence, upon attaining the first dhyāna, one is complete in every one of these merits of freedom from fault.

zh: 得初禪時具足善心功德者，約五支明功德善法，義如前說。復次，若得初禪，即具信、戒、捨、定、聞、慧等善心也。
en: As for being complete in the merit of a wholesome mind upon attaining the first dhyāna: this is clarified with reference to the five factors' own merit and wholesome dharma, the sense of which is as already given above. Furthermore, upon attaining the first dhyāna, one is also complete in such wholesome states of mind as faith, moral discipline, generosity, concentration, learning, and wisdom.

The four-by-four grid of practitioner types (regress/abide/progress/penetrate, each itself capable of regressing, abiding, progressing, or penetrating from wherever it lands) is the same combinatorial move fascicle 3's closing section made with unpredictable dhyāna-arising — demonstrating, by simply continuing to subdivide, that attainment is not a ladder climbed once and kept, but a genuinely unstable state whose trajectory depends on ongoing diligence or heedlessness. That the text flags "in this latter age, those prone to regression are many" is a rare moment of the treatise commenting directly on the difficulty of its own historical moment rather than describing the dharma in the abstract. The merits close on the same two-fold pattern used for verifying wholesome capacity back in fascicle 3 — freedom from fault paired with positive wholesome qualities — confirming that the first dhyāna is being assessed by exactly the same diagnostic apparatus already built for wholesome roots generally, not some separate standard. This closes the whole of the first dhyāna.

quiz.q: According to the Yingluo Sūtra, what are the cause and the substance of concentration in the first dhyāna?
options: the five factors are the cause; the sixth, the silent mind, is the substance, taken as the effect
quiz.why: "Some say: 'the four factors serve as the cause, and the subsequent factor of one-pointedness of mind serves as the effect' — but this has no textual basis. Here, following the Yingluo Sūtra's own explanation of the dhyāna-factors, the five factors serve as the cause, and the sixth ... serves as the substance of concentration — taking this substance itself as the effect."

quiz.q: According to the treatise cited, how many grades of depth do the Buddha's disciples have in cultivating dhyāna?
options: lower, middle, upper, each in three — nine grades; examined finely, measureless
quiz.why: "When the Buddha's disciples cultivate the various dhyānas, there is a lower, a middle, and an upper grade ... separating out each of these three grades into three further grades in turn, there are nine grades of shallowness and depth in all. Examined finely, there should be measureless grades beyond even this."

quiz.q: Non-Buddhists also have depths of concentration. Why are these not spoken of in grades?
options: their minds are coarse and unaware within concentration, and they do not cultivate uncontaminated wisdom to illuminate it
quiz.why: "Non-Buddhist practitioners, too, attain concentrations with their own shallowness and depth, though this is not spoken of in terms of grades for them, since their minds are coarse, unable to perceive it within concentration itself, and, not cultivating the uncontaminated wisdom that illuminates it, the mind fails to become aware of it at all."

quiz.q: If only one or two of the sixteen sensations arise, can it still be called the first dhyāna?
options: yes, but not "complete"; all sixteen together is the complete and superior first dhyāna
quiz.why: "The first dhyāna is of two kinds: complete; and incomplete. If all sixteen sensations arise together in full, this is precisely the complete first dhyāna, and is superior; but if only one or two sensations arise, this too may be named the first dhyāna."

quiz.q: What are the four kinds of practitioners on realizing the first dhyāna, and what is "penetrating through"?
options: regressing, abiding, progressing, penetrating; penetrating is bringing forth the uncontaminated in this very concentration and reaching nirvāṇa
quiz.why: "At the time the first dhyāna is realized, there are four kinds of practitioner, differing in capacity — those prone to regression; those who abide; those who progress; and those who penetrate through ... some people, upon attaining the first dhyāna, within this very concentration, at once bring forth the uncontaminated attainment ... penetrating through all the way to nirvāṇa."

quiz.q: Which kind of practitioner does the text say is most common in the latter age?
quiz.why: Of those prone to regression, the loss is either regained or not, "owing to some obstructing dharma from the past or the present life. In this latter age, those prone to regression of this kind are many."

quiz.q: According to the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra, the first dhyāna is "freedom" and "completeness." Freedom from what, completeness in what?
options: freedom from the five hindrances; completeness in the five factors
quiz.why: "Hence the Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says: 'The first dhyāna is named both freedom and completeness. As for freedom: this means freedom from the five hindrances. As for completeness: this means completeness in the five factors.'"

quiz.q: Why does attaining the first dhyāna free one from the hindrance of drowsiness?
options: body and mind bright and pure, sustained by concentration, the mind not dull, delighting in the joy of the sensation
quiz.why: "As for being able to gain freedom from drowsiness: upon attaining the first dhyāna, body and mind grow bright and pure, sustained by the dharma of concentration, the mind no longer dull or disordered, delighting of itself in the joy of the tactile sensation — hence there is no drowsiness."
